title: They War-Gamed Dimming the Sun. It Went Even Worse Than You Think
gist: A UK-funded war game at Queen Mary University of London simulated a UN committee coordinating on solar geoengineering, and no deal was reached as US-China mistrust, disinformation and a covert fossil-fuel-backed NGO overwhelmed scientific advice. Organizers concluded strategic competition and sovereignty, not climate concerns, drove outcomes, while real-world moves from Stardust, Musk, US think tanks and the UK suggest the issue is arriving fast.

themes.theme: Great-power distrust and the arms-race dynamic

insights.claim: In the simulation, US and China players refused any deal that constrained research in their 'national interest' or let the rival lead technologically; a US Army major summarized the stance as worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Nielsen
insights.so_what: Zero-sum framing between the superpowers makes a binding international regime unlikely.

insights.claim: Mutual suspicion left all parties believing the others were racing to build geoengineering capability even though, by design, China was not conducting experiments, showing how misperception alone can fuel an arms race.

insights.so_what: Perceived rather than actual programs can drive R&D escalation and the need for transparency and monitoring.

insights.claim: Stardust CEO Yanai Yedvab says lobbying is getting easier because most policymakers are already aware of the technology, and the company says it will not run large-scale outdoor experiments before global governance exists while acknowledging national interests will play out.
insights.speaker: Yanai Yedvab
insights.so_what: The company's self-restraint pledge depends on governance that the war game suggests is unlikely, a risk for its business model.
